analysis.one_liner: Caps rent-to-own fees at retail credit-sale limits and applies credit-law protections to those deals.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being referred to the House Financial Services Committee and its consumer credit subcommittee in July 2001, it died there when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let customers pay weekly for furniture and appliances until they own them, but the bills often end up costing far more than the item's store price. This bill would cap rent-to-own interest and fees at what state law allows on a regular credit sale of the same item, require stores to display the cash price and annual rate on the goods themselves, extend credit and debt-collection protections to customers, and let customers sue for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income and minority consumers, the people the bill's findings say the rent-to-own industry primarily targets, who would gain disclosure of the item's true cash price and total cost, fee caps matching normal retail credit sales, warranty rights, and protection from abusive collection practices.

how_it_helps.text: Caps rent-to-own interest, finance charges, and fees at the levels state law allows for a credit sale or retail installment sale of the same or a similar item.
Requires tags on goods in the store and written contracts to show the cash price, the annual percentage rate, the number and size of payments, and the total of payments needed to own the item.

Extends to rent-to-own customers the same warranty protections as retail installment buyers, and applies the Truth in Lending Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and Fair Credit Reporting Act to these transactions.

Bars abusive collection practices such as threats of criminal prosecution, coercion, harassment, and deceptive representations, with the Federal Trade Commission empowered to enforce and customers entitled to statutory damages of $250 to $2,500 per violation plus attorney fees.

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own dealers, whose effective charges on many contracts run well above state retail credit-sale limits and who would face new disclosure, warranty, and collection obligations plus FTC enforcement and private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves the customer's unilateral right to walk away from the contract at any time, which is the feature dealers point to when defending total charges above a credit sale's price; a customer using rent-to-own as short-term flexible rental, not a path to ownership, loses some of that flexibility's value once fees are capped and the deal is treated like credit.
The bill still lets dealers add a termination fee of up to 5 percent of the cash price and recovery fees for unreturned goods, so some costs remain on top of the capped charges.

Capping charges and adding liability costs could reduce store availability or raise base prices in low-income neighborhoods where rent-to-own is sometimes the only option for people without store credit or savings; the bill's own findings frame these customers as its target audience, so any contraction in service hits the people it is meant to help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward extension of protections credit buyers already have to a customer base that, per the bill's own findings, is largely low-income and rarely gets them. The main cost falls on dealers whose contracts often cost several times the cash price; the main risk to customers is that tighter economics could shrink store options in some neighborhoods. On the whole the protections outweigh the costs, and the design keeps the walk-away right that distinguishes rent-to-own from installment buying.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which sent it to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, and it never advanced further before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the Rent-To-Own Reform Act of 2001 on July 12, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

On July 31, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and the action record shows no further movement — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the 107th Congress.
The bill had 13 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats.

The bill's findings state that the rent-to-own industry targets low-income and minority neighborhoods, that most customers intend to own the goods, and that dealers often fail to disclose key terms, charge excessive fees, and withhold protections that retail installment buyers get under state and federal law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own dealers, who kept charging fees above state credit-sale limits on contracts without federal disclosure, warranty, or collection protections for their customers.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote its findings that rent-to-own dealers target low-income and minority neighborhoods and withhold protections retail credit buyers get.

against.name: Financial Services Committee and subcommittee leadership
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over consumer credit legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and never scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 18 months remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Rent-to-own industry
against.what_they_did: The industry had long lobbied to keep rent-to-own defined as a lease rather than a credit sale, the legal distinction this bill would have erased by applying credit-sale fee caps and credit laws to the transactions.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were Democrats, but no vote was ever taken and no opposition appears in the record, so the partisan split cannot be measured.

industries.note: Dealers' business model relies on weekly payments that commonly total several times the item's cash price, without the fee caps, APR disclosure, warranties, and debt-collection rules that apply to ordinary credit sales. The bill would cap those charges at state credit-sale levels and expose dealers to FTC enforcement and statutory damages, so its interest ran directly against the customers it would protect.
The bill would limit rent-to-own dealers to the credit insurance types and premiums state law allows on retail installment sales, cutting off above-cap premiums on these transactions.
